## A Thursday afternoon with the tea trolley

On my first Thursday at Wensum Vale Hospice, I spilled an entire jug of milk over the tea trolley.

A patient called Pat laughed so much that someone had to bring her a tissue. She told me it was the best afternoon she’d had in a month. I can’t claim that was the result I’d intended, but it did make the rest of my first shift less frightening.

I started volunteering in March 2022, about eighteen months after I retired. I’d spent 41 years keeping books, mostly for a builders’ merchant in Dereham, and when that stopped I found I had no particular reason to go out most weeks. I drifted a bit. Having somewhere to be on a Thursday helped with that.

The tea trolley goes round the day therapy unit from 1.30 to 4pm. There are usually about 14 to 18 patients in on a Thursday. Some come for the art group or a hand massage; some come for a bit of company. Most go home afterwards.

Mr Hollis, a retired signalman, takes two sugars and tells me about the 1953 floods every week. The details are slightly different each time. I’ve stopped correcting the dates.

The bourbon biscuits always go first, so we now hide a packet for the late group. I think that counts as forward planning rather than theft.

People sometimes imagine that volunteering at a hospice must be terribly sad, or that you need to know something about nursing. You don’t need any nursing skills for the trolley. You do need to be able to push it, remember who takes what and listen. It turns out that 41 years of keeping ledgers straight is quite useful when it comes to remembering how people take their tea.

Thursdays are mostly noisy and rather jolly. There are hard days too, and I wouldn’t pretend otherwise. When they happen, the staff look after us volunteers as well as the patients.

There are four of us on a rota meant for six at the moment. Two volunteers left over the summer: one moved to Sheffield to be near her grandchildren, and the other needed a knee operation. We could do with two more people to join us.

The commitment is **one Thursday afternoon a fortnight, from 1.30 to 4pm**. Bridget, our volunteer coordinator, does the induction, which takes about two hours. There’s also a short online food hygiene course, paid for by the hospice.

If you’ve ever thought you might like to help but weren’t sure what would be involved, come along to the **volunteer open afternoon on Tuesday 24 November at 2pm in the Willow Room**. There will be tea and biscuits, and no obligation. It would be lovely to see at least two of you there.

If you can’t make it, you can ring Bridget on the volunteering line instead.
